analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal air pollution limits on ethylene oxide, a cancer-causing gas, emitted by sterilization plants.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Ethylene oxide is a gas used to sterilize about half of all medical devices, and EPA's 2016 scientists assessment found it far more carcinogenic than previously believed. This bill would have forced the EPA, within 180 days, to rewrite its emission standards for sterilization plants based on that 2016 cancer assessment, apply the strictest available control technology to exhaust vents, and publicly disclose any violations within 30 days. If EPA failed to disclose a violation, its own Inspector General would have to investigate. The bill died in committee without any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school near ethylene oxide sterilization plants, which in the sponsor's home district included the Willowbrook, Illinois area where residents had learned of elevated cancer risk from local emissions.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to revise ethylene oxide emission standards within 180 days based on its own 2016 assessment of the gas as a carcinogen, rather than leaving older, weaker standards in place [S2][S3].
Applies maximum achievable control technology — the strictest emission controls the Clean Air Act requires — to chamber exhaust vents at sterilization facilities [S2][S3].

Requires the EPA to notify the public within 30 days of learning of a violation, with an automatic Inspector General investigation if it fails to do so, so residents are not left in the dark about emissions near their homes [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The companies that operate ethylene oxide sterilization plants would bear the cost of installing and maintaining stricter emission controls, and those costs could pressure some facilities to curtail or shut down operations.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a hard 180-day deadline for rewriting the standards, giving the EPA and affected facilities little time to assess technical feasibility, which could force costly retrofits or closures on short notice [S3].

Because ethylene oxide sterilization is the main way medical devices and supplies are sterilized, shutting or restricting plants for failure to meet the new standards could disrupt the supply of sterile medical products — a tradeoff the bill does not address [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is real and specific: residents near these plants were being exposed to a potent carcinogen under standards based on an outdated cancer assessment. The costs — retrofit expense and possible plant closures — fall on a small number of facility operators, though closures could ripple into medical supply chains. The bill's main flaw is its rigid 180-day timeline rather than its goal.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Schneider introduced the bill on November 28, 2018, with Reps. Bill Foster and Dan Lipinski of Illinois as the only cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which took no further action on it [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of ethylene oxide sterilization plants avoided a legally binding deadline to tighten emissions controls and publicly disclose violations, and the EPA avoided a mandated 180-day rewrite of its standards. Residents near the plants gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Brad Schneider
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring tighter ethylene oxide emission standards and public notice of violations.

for.name: Reps. Bill Foster and Dan Lipinski

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the final weeks of the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or recorded opposition exist; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Illinois Democrats, and the bill died in committee without a recorded position from either party.

industries.note: The bill would force ethylene oxide sterilization plants to install the strictest available emission controls and publicly disclose violations, raising their operating costs and compliance risk. Residents near these plants were exposed to a known carcinogen under outdated standards, so the industry's interest in avoiding tighter controls ran against the health of those communities.

They depend on ethylene oxide sterilization for much of their product supply, so new standards could raise costs or disrupt capacity if plants curtail operations. Stricter, transparently enforced standards also reduce the risk of sudden community-driven shutdowns like the Willowbrook controversy, which is the greater threat to their supply chain.
